summary: A framework document that classifies the approaches and issues for running IP over ATM networks, to help focus the IP over ATM working group. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Several groups proposed different ways of running IP over ATM, and this memo sorts them out. It gives the vocabulary, lists the choices that matter, and describes where each proposal sits in the framework. It is a map of the design space, not a specification to implement.

questions: how does ip run over atm

what is the classical ip model over atm
subtitle: A framework for comparing the many ways of running IP over ATM, and the trade-offs behind them.

tldr.problem: The IP over ATM working group had a diverse set of proposals on the table, some no longer under active consideration, and no shared way to talk about how they differed.
tldr.mechanism: The memo sets out a taxonomy: a set of definitions, the parameters along which proposals differ, the encapsulation options, the connection oriented trade-offs, and how direct connections across subnet boundaries are made.
tldr.outcome: It then places the main proposals, including Classical IP, NHRP, the Peer Model and the Integrated Model, inside that framework, and summarises the documents the working group produced.

today: RFC 1932 is an Informational memo from April 1996, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a framework for comparing the IP over ATM proposals of the time, and it describes NHRP and the IPMC documents as work in progress rather than finished specifications.

sections.title: Introduction: What the Framework Is For
sections.content:
The IP over ATM Working Group of the IETF is chartered to develop standards for routing and forwarding IP packets over ATM subnetworks. This document provides a classification, or taxonomy, of the IP over ATM options and issues, and then describes the various proposals in those terms. Its intent is to help clarify the differences between proposals and identify common features, so that the group can converge on a smaller and more mutually compatible set of standards.

The memo works as a set of reference points. Section 2 defines terms, section 3 sets out the parameters of the taxonomy, section 4 covers the options for low level encapsulation, section 5 the tradeoffs between connection oriented and connectionless approaches, section 6 the means of providing direct connections across IP subnet boundaries, section 7 a proposal to extend IP routing so that such connections work, section 8 the prominent proposals and their relationship to the framework, and section 9 how the documents of the working group and of related groups map onto the models.

ATM is the connection oriented network technology under discussion. Its ATM Adaptation Layers, the AALs, specify the quality of service and the connection mode, and the models described here assume an underlying connection oriented service. Two kinds of virtual circuit appear throughout: permanent, or PVC, and switched, or SVC. The PVC environment requires either static tables for the mapping between ATM and IP addresses or the use of inverse ARP, while the SVC environment requires ARP functionality to be provided.
sections.plainLanguage: The working group had many competing proposals on the table. This memo gives them a common set of words and a common set of questions, so that the proposals can be compared and narrowed down.

sections.title: Definitions and Terminology
sections.content:
The memo defines the vocabulary the rest of the document depends on. A host, or end system, delivers and receives IP packets but does not relay them. A router, or intermediate system, does the same and also relays IP packets among systems. An IP subnet is a set of members that can all transmit packets to each other directly, without forwarding by intermediate entities; no two members are considered closer in the IP topology than any other, so from the point of view of routing and forwarding a subnet is atomic, though repeaters, hubs, bridges or switches may sit between the physical interfaces of its members. A bridged IP subnet is one in which two or more physically separate media are made to appear as a single IP subnet, using either MAC level bridging or proxy ARP. A broadcast subnet supports an arbitrary number of hosts and routers and can transmit a single IP packet to all of them. A multicast capable subnet supports sending a packet that reaches a subset of the destinations on the subnet, with setup either sender initiated or leaf initiated; ATM UNI 3.0 and UNI 3.1 support only sender initiated, while IP supports leaf initiated join. A Non-Broadcast Multiple Access, or NBMA, subnet supports an arbitrary number of hosts and routers but does not natively support a convenient multi-destination connectionless transmission.

Two terms describe what happens above the subnet. IP forwarding is the process of receiving a packet and using a very low overhead decision to decide how to handle it: the packet may be delivered locally, or forwarded externally, in which case the process also chooses the outgoing interface and either removes one media layer encapsulation and replaces it with another or modifies fields in it. IP routing is the exchange of information that makes the information needed for a correct forwarding decision available. IP address resolution is the quasi-static mapping between an IP address on the local IP subnet and a media address on the local subnet, and ARP is the protocol that supports it.

The memo then names the two techniques used to get end-to-end connectivity. One allows direct connectivity across classic IP subnet boundaries, which certain NBMA media including ATM support. The other is IP routing and IP forwarding. In essence the first technique extends IP address resolution beyond the boundaries of the IP subnet, while the second interconnects IP subnets. Large internetworks, and in particular the Internet, are unlikely to be made of a single medium or a star topology with a single medium at the centre, and within a large network supporting a common medium, IP routing and forwarding must always be accommodated if the internetwork is larger than the NBMA network.
sections.plainLanguage: The terms matter because two of them are often confused. A subnet is a group of machines that can all reach each other directly. Routing is how traffic gets between subnets, and address resolution is how a machine finds the hardware address of a neighbour.

sections.title: Encapsulations and Lower Layer Identification
sections.content:
Two issues matter here, and they are somewhat orthogonal: how data is encapsulated, and how the endpoints of a virtual circuit are identified. In conventional LAN technologies the encapsulation wrapped around a packet of data typically defines the path for multiplexing and demultiplexing within the source and destination nodes, for example the Ethertype field of an Ethernet packet, so the choice of the protocol endpoint inside the destination node is carried in band. As multiplexing moves towards ATM and away from the LLC/SNAP mechanism, a greater burden falls on the call setup and teardown capacity of the ATM network, which raises questions about the scalability of these lower level multiplexing options.

With the ATM Forum UNI version 3.1 service, the choice of endpoint within a destination node is made out of band, during the call setup phase, independently of any in-band encapsulation. The B-LLI information element allows layer 2 or layer 3 entities to be specified as a circuit's endpoint. Faced with an incoming SETUP message, the called party searches locally for an AAL user that claims to provide the service of the layer named in the B-LLI, and if one is found the circuit is accepted, assuming other conditions such as quality of service requirements are also met. The obvious approach for IP environments is to specify the Internet Protocol layer as the circuit's endpoint and place IP packets into AAL service data units. This is called VC multiplexing or Null Encapsulation, because it terminates a circuit through an AAL instance directly on a layer 3 endpoint. It has a limitation in environments that need several layer 3 protocols between the same two ATM endpoints, because each pair of layer 3 protocol entities that wish to exchange packets needs its own circuit.

RFC 1483 notes that VC multiplexing is possible but describes an alternative called LLC/SNAP encapsulation, which allows any set of protocols uniquely identified by an LLC/SNAP header to be multiplexed onto a single circuit. The header is 8 bytes: the first three bytes say the payload is a routed non-ISO protocol data unit, and the organizationally unique identifier of 0x00-00-00 says the protocol identifier is taken from the EtherType associated with IP packets, 0x800. ARP packets are multiplexed the same way, with a protocol identifier of 0x806 instead of 0x800. Whatever layer terminates a circuit carrying LLC/SNAP encapsulated traffic must know how to parse the AAL service data units to retrieve the packets. The recently approved signalling standards for IP over ATM are more explicit: the default SETUP message used to establish IP over ATM circuits must carry a B-LLI specifying an ISO 8802/2 layer 2 entity as each circuit's endpoint, and there is no information in the SETUP message about the identity of the layer 3 protocol that asked for the circuit, so the terminating entity cannot know which higher layers are the packet destinations until the packets start arriving.

Two further encapsulations were discussed in the working group, and both largely or totally eliminate IP header overhead. TULIP, TCP and UDP over Lightweight IP, assumes single hop reachability between IP entities: after name resolution, address resolution and SVC signalling, an implicit binding is established between entities in the two hosts, and full IP headers, including the source and destination addresses, are not needed in each data packet. Only the IP protocol field is carried, everything else being bound at call setup time. TUNIC, TCP and UDP over a Nonexistent IP Connection, carries no network layer information at all; the binding is between two applications using TCP or UDP directly over AAL5 on a dedicated circuit, and in that case the IP protocol field has no useful dynamic function. These two models were discussed at the July 1993 IETF meeting in Amsterdam but were not fully defined by the working group.

The memo places the four on a continuum, which is simply a matter of how much is moved from in-stream demultiplexing to call setup demultiplexing. SNAP/LLC moves nothing to the setup message and demultiplexes on the source and destination address, the protocol family, the protocol and the ports. Null encapsulation moves the protocol family to the setup message. TULIP moves the source and destination address, the protocol family and the protocol, leaving the ports to be demultiplexed in the stream. TUNIC variant A also moves the protocol to setup, leaving only the ports. TUNIC variant B moves everything, so nothing is demultiplexed in the stream at all.
sections.plainLanguage: The header carried on each packet can be made smaller as more information moves into the call setup. The trade-off is that the setup has to carry it, and the receiving end must be told in advance what to expect.

sections.title: Connection Oriented and Connectionless Trade-offs
sections.content:
Both approaches have advantages and disadvantages, and strong advocates of pure connection oriented and pure connectionless architectures had argued intensely. The memo's point is that IP over ATM does not need to be purely one or the other. ATM with basic AAL 5 service is connection oriented, the IP layer above ATM is connectionless, and on top of IP much of the traffic is carried by TCP, a reliable end-to-end connection oriented protocol. A fundamental question is how far it is beneficial to map different flows above IP into separate connections below IP. At one end, IP would stay highly connectionless and set up single circuits between routers that are adjacent on an IP subnet and between which there was active traffic, multiplexing all traffic between them on one circuit. At the other end, a separate circuit would be created for each identifiable flow, so every unique TCP or UDP address and port pair would need a new circuit.

ATM offers quality of service and traffic management capabilities well suited to certain services, and it may be advantageous to use a separate circuit for them. Other IP services, such as DNS, are ill suited to connection oriented delivery, because they normally last a very short time, typically one packet in each direction, and short transactions may also be poorly suited because of the setup and state overhead. ATM quality of service and traffic management may in turn be poorly suited for elastic traffic, which is traffic that can be sent at whatever rate the network can carry.

The middle ground sets up circuits only when something indicates one is needed. RSVP, the resource reservation protocol, or another indication can say that a circuit is needed and what quality of service parameters are appropriate. Short duration UDP traffic such as DNS is forwarded hop by hop, because RSVP is unlikely to precede it. Short duration TCP traffic such as SMTP is forwarded hop by hop unless RSVP says otherwise. Elastic traffic such as bulk TCP transfer is forwarded hop by hop by default, though RSVP information, local configuration about TCP port number usage, or a local method for passing quality of service information from the application to the IP and ATM driver may allow or suggest direct circuits. Real time traffic such as audio and video is forwarded hop by hop unless RSVP indicates otherwise, since RSVP carries the quality of service requirements, and a local decision can be made about whether a separate circuit serves that quality of service better.

A pure connectionless approach forwards everything hop by hop and uses queueing algorithms implemented at the IP layer to support reservations such as those RSVP specifies. The memo notes that the work on how quality of service requirements might be expressed, and how local decisions about them might be made, belongs to the Integrated Services Working Group and the Reservation Protocol Working Group, and that the IP over ATM working group can make more rapid progress if it concentrates on how direct connections are established.
sections.plainLanguage: Setting up a connection costs time and state, so it pays only for traffic that needs it. Short lookups and bulk transfers are better off going the ordinary way; a video stream is not.

sections.title: Crossing IP Subnet Boundaries and the Routing Loop Problem
sections.content:
A single IP subnet does not scale well to a large size. The techniques that extend the size of an IP subnet in other media include MAC layer bridging and proxy ARP bridging. MAC layer bridging alone does not scale well, because protocols such as ARP rely on the media broadcast to exchange address resolution information. Most bridges improve scaling by capturing ARP packets, keeping their contents and distributing that information among bridging peers, and the ARP information gathered from replies is broadcast only where explicit requests are made. This technique is known as proxy ARP. It improves scaling by reducing broadcast traffic, but still has scaling problems: if the bridged IP subnet is part of a larger internetwork, a routing protocol is needed to indicate what destinations lie beyond the IP subnet, unless a statically configured default route is used, and a default route only suits a very simple topology and creates a single point of failure. Because internets of enormous size create scaling problems for routing protocols, the component networks of such large internets are often partitioned into areas, autonomous systems or routing domains, and routing confederacies.

For NBMA media like ATM there are advantages to creating direct connections across the entire underlying NBMA network, which leads to the need to create direct connections across IP subnet boundaries. RFC 1620 describes the problems of doing so in greater detail. The Routing over Large Clouds working group has identified persistent routing loop problems that can occur if protocols which lose information critical to path vector routing loop suppression are used to make direct connections across subnet boundaries. The problems arise when a destination network that is not on the NBMA network is reachable through different routers attached to that network, which happens with proposals that carry reachability information but not the full path attributes needed for inter-AS path suppression, or not the full metrics needed for intra-AS routing. NHRP assumes that routers do run routing protocols, and that forwarding tables built by those protocols result in a steady state loop-free forwarding situation. It runs in addition to the routing protocols and provides the information that lets several IP hops be eliminated when traversing an NBMA network. The memo notes that truncating path information in path vector protocols such as BGP, or losing metric information in distance vector protocols such as RIP, could result in persistent forwarding loops, and that such loops could occur without ATM and without NHRP.

The memo works through an example. Host 1 sends traffic toward Host 2; in practice host routes would not be used, so the destination for routing purposes is Subnet 3. The traffic travels by way of Router 1, which establishes a cut-through circuit to the next hop on the NBMA network, Router 2, and Router 2 forwards traffic for Subnet 3 through Subnet 2 to Router 3, where it reaches Host 2. While the cut-through circuit is still up, Link 1 fails. Router 5 loses its preferred route through Router 3 and directs traffic the other way. Router 2 loses its route through Router 3 but picks up an alternate through Router 5. Router 1 is still directing traffic toward Router 2 and advertising a way to reach Subnet 3 to Subnet 1, so Router 5 and Router 2 each see a route and a loop forms.

The loop would not form if the path information carried by interdomain routing protocols such as BGP and IDRP were retained across the NBMA network, because Router 2 would reject the initial route from Router 5 on the strength of the path information; a link state protocol would not form such a loop either. Two ways of breaking the loop were discussed. A redirect would have no effect here, since Router 2 still has a route, just one with different path attributes. The second is that when a route changes in any way, the advertising cut-through router invalidates the advertisement for a time, which is similar to Poison Reverse in distance vector protocols. Without path information, Router 1 cannot tell a loop from the restoration of normal service through Link 1. Special configuration can also break the loop, by refusing to use the reverse path on Router 4 or Router 5, or by refusing to use the path through Router 5 on Router 2 unless it could not reach the NBMA network. But for loops to be prevented by special configuration at the NBMA border router, that router would need to know all the paths that could lead back to the NBMA network, and the memo notes that the same argument was once made in favour of retaining the EGP protocol defined in the now historic RFC 904, which turned out to be unmanageable, with routing problems occurring when the topology changed elsewhere.
sections.plainLanguage: Letting two machines connect directly across a subnet boundary saves hops, but it can hide the information routers use to detect loops. The memo walks through an example where the traffic ends up going round in circles, and lists the ways out.

sections.title: The Main Proposals and the Working Group's Documents
sections.content:
Several models were developed, and the memo places each in the framework. The Classical IP Model, suggested at the Spring 1993 IETF meeting, keeps the classical IP subnet architecture and simply cascades instances of IP subnets with IP-level routers at the subnet borders. Forwarding over it is straightforward using well established routing techniques. SVC-based ATM IP subnets are simplified in three ways: they limit the number of hosts that must be directly connected at any time to those that may actually exchange traffic; the ATM network can set up connections between any pair of hosts, but connectivity to the outside world is achieved only through a router, which may provide firewall functionality; and the IP subnet supports an efficient mechanism for address resolution. The issues the working group addressed for this model were encapsulation and multiplexing, in RFC 1483, the definition of an address resolution server, in RFC 1577, the default maximum transmission unit, in RFC 1626, support for IP multicasting, interim SVC parameters such as quality of service parameters and time-out values, and signalling and negotiation of parameters such as MTU size and encapsulation method, in RFC 1755. RFC 1577 is also applicable to PVC-based subnets, where full mesh PVC connectivity is required.

The Next Hop Resolution Protocol, a work in progress defined by the Routing over Large Clouds working group, performs address resolution to achieve direct connections across IP subnet boundaries and can supplement RFC 1577 ARP. It can also perform a proxy address resolution to give the address of the border router serving a destination off the NBMA network when that destination is served by a single router on the NBMA. As currently defined it cannot be used that way for addresses learned from routers where the same destinations may be heard at other routers, without risking persistent routing loops. The "Conventional" Model assumes that a router can relay IP packets cell by cell, with the VPI and VCI identifying a flow between adjacent routers rather than between a pair of nodes. Cell interleaving from multiple IP packets can give a latency advantage, but interleaving frames within the same VCI requires an AAL such as AAL3/4 rather than AAL5. The IP over ATM working group was not considering this model, and the COLIP working group was formed to develop protocols based on it.

The Peer Model places IP routers and gateways on an addressing peer basis with corresponding entities in an ATM cloud, with IP addresses mapped algorithmically into the NSAP address space and ATM level addressing, call routing and packet formats used inside the cloud. It makes no provision for selecting a primary path and using an alternate path when the primary fails, which limits it to topologies where non-ATM networks are singly homed or where loss of backup connectivity does not matter. The memo records that the problems with the end-to-end peer model were felt to be much harder than those of any other model, and that it was not an initial priority of the working group. The ATM Forum Network Layer Multiprotocol Working Group reached a similar conclusion.

The Integrated Model, proposed and under study within the Multiprotocol group of the ATM Forum, considers a single routing protocol for both IP and ATM, with a single exchange of routing information distributing topological information, and a routing computation that takes the topology, link and node characteristics of both networks into account to calculate an optimal route for IP packets over the combined topology. PNNI, the Private Network-to-Network Interface routing protocol, is a hierarchical link state routing protocol with multiple link metrics providing the various quality of service parameters available under current loading, and call route selection takes quality of service requirements into account. Using PNNI routing as an IP routing protocol raises issues about the interaction of multiple routing protocols, adaptation of PNNI to broadcast media, and support for NHRP. PNNI has provisions for carrying uninterpreted information, and a compatible extension of the base protocol could carry external routing attributes and avoid the routing loop problems.

Transition models lie between the Classical IP models and the Peer and Integrated models. Some models, most notably the Integrated Model, anticipate a mixed environment with complex routing topologies and therefore support a transition, possibly an indefinite one. Models that provide no transition support are of interest mainly to new deployments making exclusive use of ATM, or to deployments able to replace their existing networks wholesale, or willing to keep only non-ATM stub networks. The memo closes with a table setting out the working group's documents: RFC 1483 for labelling multiple protocols multiplexed over AAL5, RFC 1577 for transporting IP and ARP over AAL5 in a subnet where all nodes share a common prefix, RFC 1626 for the default IP maximum transmission unit over AAL5, RFC 1755 for the use of ATM call control signalling, the IPMC documents for IP multicast in the Classical IP model, and NHRP for finding the NBMA next hop address of a destination.
sections.plainLanguage: Each proposal is a different answer to the same question: how much of the old IP model to keep. Some keep it entirely and add ATM underneath. Others map IP addresses into ATM addresses and let the two networks peer with each other.

items.title: Classical IP
items.text: Cascaded IP subnets with routers at the borders, using ordinary IP routing.

items.title: NHRP
items.text: Resolves addresses so a host can connect directly across subnet boundaries.

items.title: Conventional
items.text: Relays packets cell by cell; needs an AAL such as AAL3/4 to interleave frames.

items.title: Peer
items.text: Maps IP addresses into the ATM address space and peers with the ATM network.

items.title: Integrated
items.text: Uses one routing protocol for IP and ATM across a combined topology.

items.title: Transition
items.text: Sits between the Classical and the Peer and Integrated models, for mixed deployments.
